cells.tense: You are sitting in the middle of a threshold and you are still able to tell what here matters.
cells.ask: Name one thing that matters and one that no longer does, say it to yourself, then hand the next hour to something that can hold it.
cells.core:
You know what matters here, and you're not pretending the rest doesn't. There's a difference between wanting to leave something behind and actually walking on — and you're awake to which is which. That could look like leaving a group, or not; what it is, is that you've sorted some of what you carry into what still connects you and what doesn't.

That sorting is what makes the rest possible. You said the thing that matters without defending it, and no one had to agree with you for the ground under you to hold. What comes after that is quieter: you keep holding what matters and let what doesn't rest. The cost is you may lose a name for one of these rooms. That's part of the movement, not a problem.
cells.sheetLine: You know what matters here and you've stopped defending the rest.
cells.verb: walking on from what no longer carries the connection
cells.place: in the room where you know what matters

cells.tense: You are standing past the crossing before it has been made, sorting in a future that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Write down what you think you'll need to leave behind, and build one small structure from something you can already reach.
cells.core:
You're already sorting what to keep and what to leave, and you're sorting it ahead of time. Somewhere out front there is an arrangement where the ground is clear and the rooms are set — and you're bracing for it, rehearsing the leaving before anything has asked you to go. What actually keeps you connected to the people in front of you is not the same as the plan you've made for them.

When you catch yourself patching over what doesn't fit, the leaving has run ahead of the living again. You don't have to tear anything up. Pick one thing you can build from what's already here. The bracing costs you the connection it was meant to protect.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a threshold you have already crossed, waiting for permission that stopped being needed.
cells.ask: Take one pattern that has been running your attention lately, write down what it's doing, and put a question about it on the page.
cells.core:
You know more about what matters than your daily attention admits. It shows in how fast you catch on, how particular your taste is about what deserves time — but you're not banking on it. You watch from the edge instead of standing in the room, and from the edge you can still see what matters without spending anything on it.

The curious part is you're not out of reach. You're close enough to see it and far enough not to act on it. Look at one pattern that has been taking your attention lately, write down what it's doing, and let the question sit. A clear line can come before a decision does.
cells.sheetLine: You see what matters and you're not betting on it.

cells.tense: You are already keeping what matters to the people around you, and calling it something that happens on its own.
cells.ask: Say one thing out loud that you've only been noticing, and let someone else keep it.
cells.core:
You're already keeping what matters to the people around you — the timing, the phrasing, the things that get let pass — and talking about it as if it were the room's doing. You know what to attend to here, and you've been attending to it without crediting the one who chooses. That eye is real and it's working. It's why things land the way they do, and why people bring you the unfinished version first.

Nothing here needs fixing. The eye just runs without your name on it. Say the thing out loud once, in your own voice, and let someone else hold it. What you've been noticing becomes something another person can meet you in, and you get to be the one who put it there.
cells.sheetLine: You're already keeping what matters here. Say so.

attempts.check: The record can't support that the person has actually left anyone or any group — Passage only says a threshold of shared meaning is being reached, so the cells must locate a moment of sorting rather than state a history. A reader could reasonably say no one has been left at all, and the Too Much and Too Little asks still work if the read is wrong: both are doable acts on what matters now, not repairs of the past. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about recognising that deeper connection lies elsewhere — real thresholds usually aren't that legible from inside, so it stays out.
